VIPIN SINGH B BLOCK- 29, Add"- GAL 1 NO-, D.C.M COLONY, IBRAHIM PUR EXT. DELHI-110084 .......................Accused JUDGMENT CNR No. DLNT020059342023 CC NI ACT 607/2023 Date of Insititution 25.03.2023 Offence alleged Under Section 138 NI Act Plea of the accused Not pleaded guilty Final Order Convicted Date of Decision 07.05.2025 Digitally signed by HIMANSHI TYAGI HIMANSHI CC NI ACT 607/2023 TYAGI Date: 2of17 2025.05.07 17:49:46 +0530 BRIEF FACTS RELEVANT FOR THE DECISION OF THE CASE ARE AS UNDER: (1.) Succinctly stated, the facts of the case are that the complainant is wife of Late Satyanarain Sah who was as labour contractor. It is alleged that in the year 2018, accused represented himself to be the owner of the property in Nangli Poona, Delhi to the husband of complainant and approached him to hire labourers in order to construct three storey building at his property. For this work, accused and husband of complainant mutually agreed upon consideration amount of about Rs. 20,00,000/. The husband of complainant provided labourers for construction and as such construction started but unfortunately during the construction, husband of complainant passed away on 08.02.2019 and only 95% construction work could be completed by him before his demise. Thereafter, remaining work was completed by brother-in-law of complainant namely Madan Sah. Accused had only paid Rs. 12,50,000/- in cash to the husband of complainant before his demise and the balance amount of Rs. 7,50,000/ remained unpaid. For seeking the payment of this balance amount, the complainant approached accused person repeatedly but accused deferred to pay on one pretext or another. The complainant thus took assistance of few neighbours and held a meeting with the accused wherein they entered into a settlement and accused agreed to pay Rs. 5,50,000 /- in satisfaction of total outstanding dues of Rs. 7,50,000/- to the complainant. In pursuance of settlement, on 25.07.2019, accused issued three cheques bearing no. 000173, 000174 and 000175 drawn on Bank of Baroda, Azadpur, Delhi for Rs. 2,00,000/-, 2,00,000/- and 2,50,000/- respectively to discharge his liability to complainant but these cheques were returned back with remarks "Payment Stopped By Drawer" all vide memos dated 13.02.2023. Complainant sent a legal demand notice dated 21.02.2023 to the accused but despite its delivery, accused neither replied nor paid the outstanding dues. Hence the complainant filed the present case. Digitally signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI Date: TYAGI 2025.05.07 17:49:48 +0530 CC NI ACT 607/2023 3of17 EVIDENCE AND PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE COURT: (2.) Upon appreciation of presummoning evidence, accused was summoned by the Ld Predecessor vide order dated 24.06.2023 for an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Act. Thereafter, on the 01.11.2023, notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. for the offence u/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act was served upon him by the Ld Predecessor to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Further, he submitted that he had issued the cheques in question as blank signed security cheques and he did not fill the particulars of the cheques and had given the cheques 4-5 years ago to the complainant's husband Narayan and he did not owe any liability towards the complainant. He admitted his signature on the cheques in question and denied the delivery of the legal notice of demand. Thereafter, the accused was permitted to cross examine the complainant and the matter was listed for evidence. (3.) The complainant has relied upon following documents:- Copy of her aadhar card Ex. CW-1/1, copy of aadhar card of accused Ex. CW-1/2, original settlement document Ex. CW-1/3, original cheque bearing no. 000173 Ex. CW-1/4, return memo of cheque bearing no. 000173 Ex. CW-1/4A, original cheque bearing no. 000174 Ex. CW-1/5, return memo of cheque bearing no. 000174 Ex. CW-1/5A, original cheque bearing no. 000175 Ex. CW-1/6, return memo of cheque bearing no. 000175 Ex. CW-1/6A, copy of legal demand notice Ex. CW-1/7, tracking report Ex. CW-1/8 (colly.) and original DTDC courier receipt Ex. CW-1/9 (colly.) respectively. The complainant was cross examined at length by the Ld. Counsel for accused. CE was closed vide order dated 05.03.2025 by the court and matter was fixed for statement of accused. (4.) Statement of the accused was recorded u/s 313 Cr.P.C. r/w Section 281 Cr.P.C on 16.04.2025 wherein all the incriminating circumstances appearing in evidence against the Digitally signed CC NI ACT 607/2023 by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI 4of17 Date: TYAGI 2025.05.07 17:49:51 +0530 accused were put to him wherein he denied the liability and stated that his father is the owner of the property , he had approached the husband of the complainant to procure labour for construction of around 2.5 storey and the consideration amount for the same was around Rs. 10 to 12 lacs which was paid in advance to the husband of the complainant. He further stated that after the demise of the complainant the remaining work was completed by the brother in law of the complainant and the payment for the same was done to Madan Sah. He denied the delivery of legal notice but admitted his address mentioned therein it be correct. Accused did not chose to lead DE, therefore, the matter was then listed for final arguments. ARGUMENTS: (5.) During arguments, it was averred by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant that the complainant has proved all the essential ingredients of the offence u/s 138 NI Act, that the presumption arises u/s 139 r/w section 118(a) of the Act is in her favour, the defence of the accused was a mere averment and accused has failed to rebut the presumption therefore accused is liable to be convicted u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. He relied upon the following cases:- Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan C.C. Alavi Haji Vs. Palapetty Muhammed, Hiten P. Dalal Vs. Bratindranath Banerjee , M/S. Kalamani Tex Vs. P. Balasubramanian , Subodh S. Salaskar Vs. Jayprakash M. Shah and Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel Vs. State of Gujarat . (6.) Per contra, the Ld counsel for the accused reiterated the defence of the accused given in statement u/s 313 CrPC and argued that the accused issued the cheques in question as security cheques to the husband of the complainant, he already paid the entire amount to her husband and there is no legally enforceable debt qua the cheques in question. He also argued that accused did not fill the particulars of the cheques, that the contents of Digitally signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI Date: TYAGI 2025.05.07 17:49:54 CC NI ACT 607/2023 +0530 5of17 settlement agreement are in favour of the accused, the complainant failed to prove her case beyond reasonable doubts and thus accused be acquitted. DECISION ALONG WITH BRIEF REASONS: (7.) I have perused the entire record as well as the evidence led by the complainant as well as the accused. Before finding the conviction of the accused u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, it has to be established by the complainant cumulatively that: (i) the cheque in question was issued by the accused in favour of the complainant in discharge of legally enforceable liability; (ii) presentation of the cheque to the bank within three months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (iii) a demand being made in writing by the payee or holder in due course by the issuance of a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank of the return of the cheques; and (iv) the failure of the drawer to make payment of the amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course within fifteen days of the receipt of the notice. (8.) It is a well settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that a criminal trial precedes on the presumption of innocence of the accused i.e. an accused is presumed to be innocent unless proved guilty. Thus, in the regular course, the initial burden is on the complainant/ prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused and the standard of proof for the same is beyond reasonable doubt. However, in offences under Section 138 NI Act, there is a reverse onus clause, which is contained in Sections 118 and 139 of the Act. It is pertinent to reproduce Sec.118 and Sec.139 of the N.I. Act here. (09.) Section 118 of the N.I Act provides : Digitally signed by HIMANSHI TYAGI HIMANSHI Date: TYAGI CC NI ACT 607/2023 2025.05.07 17:49:59 6of17 +0530 "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: a. of consideration - that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" (10.) Section 139 of the N.I Act further provides as follows: "Presumption in favour of holder - it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability". (11.) For the offence of Section 138 of the Act, a presumption u/s 118(a) and Section 139 has to be compulsorily raised as soon as execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon accused to prove otherwise. These presumptions shall be rebutted when only when the contrary is proved by the accused i.e. the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. A presumption is not in itself evidence but only makes a primafacie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. Presumptions under both the sections i.e. Section 118(a) and Section 139 of N.I. Act are rebuttable in nature. Once Section 139 of NI Act comes into picture, the Court presumes that the cheque was issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or liability. The effect of the presumption has been explained in a catena of judgments, including the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in, Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee ( 2001) 6 SCC 16, Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 and further in the case of Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel v. State of Gujarat & anr (Crl. Appeal No. 508/19 dated 15.03.2019). Digitally signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI TYAGI Date: CC NI ACT 607/2023 2025.05.07 17:50:02 7of17 +0530 (12.) In the case at hand, the accused has admitted his signatures upon the cheques in question in the notice served upon him under Section 251 CrPC. He also admitted correctness of the bank return memos u/s 294 Cr.P.C In his statement u/s 313 CrPC the accused denied receipt of legal notice but he admitted that his address mentioned in legal notice. In this context, it is incumbent to note that the the mandatory requirement of issue of notice in terms of clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of N.I Act stands complied with if the payee has dispatched the notice by registered post with correct address of the drawer of the cheque and the principle incorporated in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted. The accused has not disputed the address mentioned on the legal notice, though he has denied the service of the notice. In light of the judgment C.C. Alavi Haji Vs Palapetty Muhammed & Anr 2007 (6) SCC 555 passed by Hon'ble Apex court, the defence of not receiving the notice is not maintainable if the accused does not pay amount of the cheque to the complainant within 15 days of receiving the summons from the court. The accused did not do so in the present case and has failed to adduce any evidence to rebut the presumption of due service. Therefore, the accused is deemed to be served with the legal notice under section 138 N.I. Act. Accordingly, conditions No. (ii), (iii) and (iv) mentioned as above stands satisfied as. Therefore, the presentation of cheques in question bearing the signatures of accused, their dishonorment and service of legal demand notice is not under question. Once these facts are established, a presumption of the cheques having been issued in discharge of a legally sustainable liability and drawn for good consideration is raised by virtue of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of the NI Act. In this aspect, the cases cited and relied upon by the Ld counsel for the complainant, supports the case of the complainant. Therefore, at this stage, with the help of the presumption under Section 139 of the Act, the condition no (i) also stands presumed and the case of the complainant stands proved. Digitally signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI TYAGI Date: 2025.05.07 17:50:05 +0530 CC NI ACT 607/2023 8of17 (13.) When the presumption is raised in favor of the complainant, the burden shifts upon the accused to disprove the case of the complainant by rebutting the presumption raised in favour of the complainant. It is well settled that in order to rebut the presumption and shift back the burden of proof on the complainant, the accused is only required to raise a probable defence and he cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof. Therefore, the standard of proof for rebutting the presumption under Section 139 NI Act is "preponderance of probabilities." (14.) The accused, thus, has to make out a fairly plausible defence for it to be accepted to the court. The accused can do this, either by leading direct evidence in his defence or by raising doubt on the material/evidence brought on record by the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. However, at the same time, it is also to be remembered that bare denial of the existence of legally enforceable debt or other liability cannot be said to be sufficient to rebut the presumption and something which is probable has to be brought on record to shift the burden back to the complainant. (15.) Keeping these basic principles in mind, this Court shall now proceed to deal with the defence of the accused and whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption raised in favour of the complainant. DEFENCE OF NON EXISTENCE OF LEGALLY RECOVERABLE LIABILITY (16.) The central leg of the defence of the accused is that he doesn't owe any liability to the complainant as he had paid the entire amount to her husband before his death. To prove Digitally signed by HIMANSHI CC NI ACT 607/2023 HIMANSHI TYAGI 9of17 Date: TYAGI 2025.05.07 17:50:08 +0530 his this defence, he mainly relied upon the document Ex CW1/1 and the cross examination of the complainant. It is his defence that it is written in ExCW1/1 that entire settlement has taken place and he does not owe any amount. On the other hand, the Ld counsel for the complainant argued that the said document was executed after settlement and by that time accused had already handed over the cheques in question and so it states about no further liability. To decide this issue, it is pertinent as well as imminent to decipher what Ex CW1/1 states and deals with. To elucidate the contents of Ex CW1/1, the same are produced herein: "आज दिनांक 25.07. 2019 को श्री विपिन सिंह s/o श्री अजय पाल सिंह नाथूपुरा दिल्ली और श्रीमती रिंकू कु मारी w/o स्व. श्री सत्यनारायण शाह, सत्यनारायण शाह ने विपिन सिंह का नगली में मकान नंबर B- 16/17 का काम किया था उनके देहांत की अवस्था में काम का सारा हिसाब विपिन जी से हो गया है आज की तारीख में दोनों पक्ष का कोई लेनदेन नहीं रहा जो हिसाब बना वह विपिन जी ने दे दिया है सत्यनारायण का कोई भी पुराना चेक अगर किसी भी व्यक्ति के पास होगा तो उसकी कोई मानता नहीं है" (17.) As evident from bare perusal, the above document neither mentions any specific amount of settlement or liability nor is there any mention of the fact of handing over of any cheques by the accused to the complainant. There is nothing in this document about any unpaid amount or giving of cheques in question for the balance payment. It only states that remaining work was performed by brother in law of complainant and account has been settled thereafter. The exact settlement terms and settlement amount do not find any mention in this document. The careful perusal of Ex CW1/1 also shows that the contents Digitally signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI CC NI ACT 607/2023 TYAGI Date: 2025.05.07 10of17 17:50:10 +0530 of the said document are patently ambiguous. The language of Ex CW1/1 does not support contentions of any of the party in toto. Thus, it would not be safe to rely on this document as the gospel truth of the liability in question. The complainant already has presumption in his favour. Hence, it is the accused who is now relying on the contents of this document in support of his case and to rebut the presumption, though it has been filed by the complainant. None of the witnesses of Ex CW1/1 has been examined by the accused in support of his contentions regarding this document. As already stated, the language of the contents of Ex CW1/1 is vague and unclear. In such scenario, benefit of the same cannot be given to the accused and it does not aid the accused in proving his defence. (18.) The accused is thus now required to prove his defence of non existence of liability through other evidences. In this context, is pertinent to note that it is not in dispute that accused had engaged the services of the husband of the complainant for construction work at his property. He admitted the same categorically in his statement u/s 313 CrPC. The accused has not denied issuance of the cheque for the transaction of construction work to the husband of the complainant. There is no proof of payment done by the accused to the husband of the complainant for the work done by him during his lifetime. Accused has also admitted that the husband of the complainant has completed 95% of the work before his death and the remaining work was completed by the brother in law of the complainant, namely Madan Sah. However, this is where a contradiction in the answer and stand of the accused flows from. In his statement u/s 313 CrPC accused stated that for the work done by Madan Sah, he paid the amount to him. He did not state the specific amount paid to Madan Sah. On the other hand, in his answer to question no 01 in his same statement, he stated that the entire amount for the work done was paid in advance. Thus, the stand of the accused is inconsistent in this regard. There is no oral or documentary proof of the payments done to the husband of the complainant or to Madan Sah. Mere averment by the accused that he had already paid the amount, is not sufficient to rebut the presumption. Digitally signed by HIMANSHI CC NI ACT 607/2023 HIMANSHI TYAGI Date: 11of17 TYAGI 2025.05.07 17:50:14 +0530 Therefore, his defence that he had paid the entire amount and does not owe any liability is rejected. DEFENCE THAT HE ISSUED THE CHEQUES AS SECURITY CHEQUES (19.) It is also the defence of the accused that he had issued the cheques in question as security cheques to the husband of the complainant. To determine the same, it will be worthwhile to consider the law on security cheques. (20.) It has been clearly stipulated by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Suresh Chandra Goyal v. Amit Singhal (Crl.L.P. 706/2014, dated 14.05.2015) that there is no magic in the word "security cheque", such that, the moment the accused claims that the dishonoured cheque (in respect whereof, a complaint under Section 138 of the Act is preferred) was given as a "security cheque", the Magistrate would acquit the accused. It is to be noted that whenever a cheque is issued, it is presumed to be issued in discharge of liability on part of the accused, though the liability may be an existing liability or a liability which would crystallize in future. If that were not so, there would be no purpose of obtaining a security cheque from the debtor. A security cheque is issued by the debtor so that the same may be presented for payment, as and when the apprehended liability arises. Otherwise, it would not be a security cheque. Therefore, if a cheque is issued to secure any future liability arising towards the payee of the cheque for the purpose of which the cheque was issued by the drawer, the drawer cannot raise the defence that the cheque was issued for security purposes. (21.) The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd. Vs. Shruti Investments 223 (2015) DLT 343 has held that even a security cheque can form the basis of complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act, if on the date of the deposit of the post-dated Digitally signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI TYAGI Date: CC NI ACT 607/2023 2025.05.07 17:50:17 12of17 +0530 security cheque, the debt of the accused stood crystallized. The relevant extract from the judgment is reproduced below: "27. Thus, the "debt or other liability" has to be a legally enforceable debt or other liability. Neither the main provision of Section 138 , nor the explanation suggest that the debt or other liability should be in existence on the date of issuance of the cheque, i.e. on the date of its delivery to the drawee or someone on his behalf or, on the date that the cheque bears. The only reference to time in the Section, is the point of time when the cheque is returned unpaid by the drawers bank." "In my view, therefore, the scope of Section 138 NI Act would cover cases where the ascertained and crystallized debt or other liability exists on the date that the cheque is presented, and not only to case where the debt or other liability exists on the date on which it was delivered to the seller as a post-dated cheque, or as a current cheque with credit period. The liability, though, should be in relation to the transaction in respect whereof the cheque is given, and cannot relate to some other independent liability. If, on the date that the cheque is presented, the ascertained and crystallized debt or other liability relatable to the dishonoured cheque exists, the dishonor of the cheque would invite action under Section 138 NI Act. There could be situations where, for example, an issue may be raised with regard to the quality, quantity, deficiency, specifications, etc. of the goods/services supplied, or accounting. It would have to be examined on a case to case basis, whether an ascertained or crystallized debt or other liability exists, which could be enforced by resort to Section 138 NI Act, or not." (22.) In the case at hand, accused has admitted in his statement u/s 313 CrPC that he gave the cheques in question for the transaction of construction work, i.e, the transaction in question. As already stated, the accused had failed to prove that the he did not owe any Digitally signed by HIMANSHI CC NI ACT 607/2023 HIMANSHI TYAGI TYAGI Date: 13of17 2025.05.07 17:50:20 +0530 liability to the complainant at the time of the presentation of the cheque. Thus, the defence of the accused that the cheques were security cheques also fails. DEFENCE THAT ACCUSED DID NOT FILL THE PARTICULARS OF THE CHEQUES (23.) It is also the defence of the accused that he did not fill the particulars of the cheques and complainant refused to return his cheques and had misused the same to file the present case. In this regard, accused cross examined the complainant, wherein she deposed that she got the date filled buy his uncle. She thus admitted that accused had not mentioned the date. She denied the suggestion that accused had not mentioned the name and amount on the cheques. The explanation provided by her in her cross examination itself is that accused gave the cheques at the time of settlement, but did not pay the amount despite seeking time, so she finally presented the cheques three after receiving them. The accused on the other hand, has not filed any proof to show that he made demand of the return of the cheques and/or took any steps against the complainant for not returning the cheques. This gives us two versions. The one of the complainant seems more reliable as she has been subjected to cross examination and deposed the above on oath whereas the accused neither subjected himself to examination nor examined anyone else in support of his defence. (24.) Further, even if its the accused did not fill the particulars on the cheques in question , this fact alone is not sufficient to absolve the accused of his liability and does not bring out any credible defence. Even if for the sake of argument, it is considered that the accused gave blank signed cheque to the complainant, once accused had admitted his signatures on the cheque, he cannot escape his liability on the ground that particular have not been filled by him, or the signature on the cheque and the contents are filled in different writing and ink. When such a cheque containing blank is signed and handed over, it means that person signing it, has given implied authority to the holder of the Digitally cheque, to fill up the signed by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI CC NI ACT 607/2023 TYAGI Date: 14of17 2025.05.07 17:50:23 +0530 blank which he has left. It has been clearly laid down in section 20 of Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 that where one person signs and delivers to another a Negotiable Instrument either wholly blank or having written thereon incomplete Negotiable Instrument, he thereby gives, "prima facie authority to the holder thereof to make or complete, as the case may be, upon it a Negotiable Instrument". In the case of Satish Jayantilal Shah Vs. Pankaj Mashruwala & anr., 1996 Cri.L.J.3099, it has been held that : "No law provides that in case of any Negotiable Instruments, entire body has to be written by maker or drawer only." (25.) In the case of Moideen vs Johny, 2006 (2) DCR 421, it has been held that when a blank cheque is issued, the drawer gives an authority to a person to whom it is issued, to fill it at appropriate stage with necessary entries and to present it to the bank. In instant case, since the accused has admitted his signature in answer to notice u/s 251 Cr.P.C as well as his statement u/s 313 Cr.P.C, the accused cannot now dispute the contents of the cheques in question. (26.) It is trite to reiterate that the complainant is required to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt against the accused, whereas, the accused is only required to prove his defence on the basis of preponderance of probabilities. The probable defence taken by the accused may be proved either during the cross-examination of the complainant or by adducing his own evidence towards defence evidence. (27.) In the case at hand the defence of the accused remains a convenient denial of facts and a mere averment. The entire defence of the accused was verbatim and mere statements. No documentary proof or witnesses were produced, whatsoever, to substantiate his defence. The version of the accused seems highly improbable and is not Digitally signed CC NI ACT 607/2023 15of17 by HIMANSHI HIMANSHI TYAGI Date: TYAGI 2025.05.07 17:50:26 +0530 sufficient to create a reasonable doubt before this Court. I am thus of view that the defence of the accused fails and he has failed to rebut the presumption in favour of the complainant by adducing evidence or by way of pointing out inconsistencies in version of complainant. Reference can be made to the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India P. Rasiya Vs Abdul Nazer and Anr. (CrA no.1233-1235 of 2022) wherein it was held that merely by denial or merely by creation of doubt, the accused cannot be said to have rebutted the presumption as envisaged under Section 139A NI Act. (28.) In considered view of the court, the present complaint has successfully proved all the essential ingredients of Section 138 NI Act. On the other hand, the accused has failed to failed to rebut the mandatory presumption raised under Section 139 r/w 118 NI Act in favour of the complainant either on the basis of the material available on record or by adducing any cogent defence evidence except bare averments, which were not at all substantiated by any material on record. (29.) In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the above discussion, the Court is of the considered view that the accused person namely Vipin Singh is guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, he is hereby convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. (30.) Let the convict be heard on quantum of sentence. (31.) Copy of Judgment be supplied to the convict free of cost. (32.) Ordered accordingly.
